messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Bounpheng, at seventy-four, still possessed the steady hands of the master welder he had been for nearly fifty years. It was his mind, not his hands, that had begun to betray him. He came to therapy at the quiet insistence of his wife, who could no longer bear to watch him pace the house at night, his face a mask of taut exhaustion. For decades, the past had been a distant country, but now it felt like an occupying force in his own home. The event itself remained a blur of dust and noise from over half a century ago in Laos. He was a young man, fleeing his village with his family, when a military truck roared up the dirt road behind them. The memory was not a story but a series of jagged, sensory snapshots: the high-pitched whine of the engine, the taste of dirt in his mouth as he ran, the desperate, burning strain in his lungs. Because these fragments are purely sensory and lack a narrative context, similar sounds and physical sensations in his daily life have become potent cues, feeling charged with the same original threat. He remembers the wide, terrifying emptiness of the rice paddy they had to cross. The rest is missing, a void he has spent a lifetime trying not to look into.

The gaps in what he could recall were the most damning; in those empty spaces, he was certain he had hesitated, that the event happened because of the way he acted. This conviction that he was somehow to blame settled deep in his bones. The memory feels so extreme, so outside the bounds of his quiet American life, that it’s hard to believe it happened to him at all; it feels like a story about someone else, a ghost whose guilt he inherited. This sense of personal failure is twinned with a profound, simmering anger at the injustice of it all—that the men in that truck, the architects of that chaos, faced no consequences. The world, he had come to believe, was an unaccountable and dangerous place. This conviction meant he could never truly be at ease, as it redefined what constituted a threat. Because he now believed that danger could erupt without reason, formerly innocuous events—the rumble of a truck, the physical strain of his work—were no longer neutral, but instead became potential signals that the fragile peace was about to be broken.

This conviction that the world is fundamentally unjust keeps him in a constant state of alert. Because the people responsible were never punished, Bounpheng feels that danger could erupt again at any moment, and he must be the one to see it coming. He has difficulty concentrating at his workshop, his focus shattered by the slightest unexpected noise from the street. At night, he lies awake, convinced that if he falls asleep, he will miss the sign of impending disaster. This hypervigilance means his senses are always primed for danger, making him exquisitely sensitive to the very things that echo the past.

Any trigger can collapse the decades in an instant. The sound of a car accelerating too quickly down his residential street is enough to bring back a flash of the truck on the dirt road, that alien memory fragment resurfacing without context or warning. The simple feeling of being short of breath after carrying a heavy gas cylinder across the workshop floor floods him with the same primal panic he felt running across that open field. In these moments, his immediate response is to retreat. He will abandon his work in the yard and go into the cramped, windowless office, avoiding the feeling of being exposed in an open space. He quickly tries to think of something else—a welding project, his grocery list, anything to dislodge the image.

Over the years, these retreats have become a way of life. He has never spoken in detail about what happened, not even to his wife. The shame of his perceived failure makes the words impossible to form, and this silence only seems to confirm his own worst judgments about his actions that day. By pushing the memories away and refusing to give them voice, he has ensured they remain a collection of terrifying, unprocessed shards. The story has no beginning or end, only a menacing, recurring middle. The more he avoids, the more fragmented the memory becomes, and the more the fragments ambush him. The cycle has worn him down. What finally brought him to seek help was an afternoon last month when a news report about a conflict overseas came on the television. The brief footage of a military vehicle was enough to make his chest seize up. He fled to the garage, unable to breathe, certain that the danger he had been watching for all these years had finally arrived at his door. He is here now not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, exhausted by the vigilance and terrified that he is losing the fight to keep the past contained.
